{"D687/ch1/s1": {"title": "Team Roles and Responsibilities", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
ICIndividual Contributor; an engineer not in management.
PMProduct Manager; defines what gets built and prioritizes.
Tech leadEngineer responsible for technical direction of a project or team.
Team shapesa self-organizing team decides INTERNALLY how to accomplish its work — managers set the what and why, the team owns the how.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — staffing one sprint’s work

WORKED EXAMPLE — who does what on the “export feature”
• Product owner — decides WHAT and priority: “CSV export matters most; PDF can wait” — owns the backlog.
• Scrum master / team lead — owns the PROCESS: clears the blocked staging environment, keeps ceremonies running; not the boss of the code.
• Developers — own HOW: design, build, test the export.
• QA/testing role — owns verification: edge cases (10GB export? empty data?).
• DevOps role — owns the pipeline that ships it.
On student/small teams one PERSON wears several hats — the roles still exist; assign them explicitly or the unowned one (usually QA) silently vanishes.
⚠️ OWNER OF WHAT vs OWNER OF HOW
Product owner decides what/priority; the team decides how/estimates. A PO dictating implementation or a dev re-prioritizing the backlog solo are the classic dysfunction scenarios exams pose.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Software is built by teams, and teams have roles even when they are informal. Knowing who does what — and where roles overlap — is the difference between smooth collaboration and constant friction.

Core concepts

1. Engineer roles. IC engineer (writes code, fixes bugs). Senior/Staff (technical leadership, mentoring, design). Lead (project leadership, code review). Differences are responsibility scope, not skill level necessarily.

2. Cross-functional partners. Product Manager (what to build, why). Engineering Manager (people, process). Designer (UX, UI). QA (test plans, automation). Each has distinct ownership.

3. Role overlap on small teams. On a 4-person team, an engineer might do PM work and design. That is fine. Be explicit about who owns what to avoid duplicated or dropped work.

4. Shared vs owned responsibilities. Code quality is shared. Code review is shared. A specific feature has one owner. A subsystem has one tech lead. Clarity prevents chaos.

5. Stakeholders beyond the team. Customers, support, sales, legal, security. Each has a stake. Map them early so you do not get surprised at launch.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Assuming roles work the same at every company — they do not. Ask.
  • Letting role boundaries become walls — 'not my job' kills teams.
  • Forgetting non-engineering stakeholders until launch day.

Quick recap

Roles bring clarity. Map who owns what; respect ownership while staying flexible. Stakeholders extend beyond engineering.

Glossary

IC
Individual Contributor; an engineer not in management.
PM
Product Manager; defines what gets built and prioritizes.
Tech lead
Engineer responsible for technical direction of a project or team.

Team shapes: a self-organizing team decides INTERNALLY how to accomplish its work — managers set the what and why, the team owns the how. A T-shaped member has deep expertise in one area plus broad ability to help across others — the vertical bar and the horizontal bar of the T.

"}, "D687/ch1/s2": {"title": "Communication Patterns That Work", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
RFCRequest for Comments; a written proposal for technical change.
PostmortemWritten analysis of an incident or project outcome.
AsyncCommunication that does not require simultaneous presence.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — communication patterns that prevent disasters

WORKED EXAMPLE — the same blocker, handled badly vs well
Badly: Dev A is blocked on an API key for three days, says nothing (“didn’t want to bother anyone”), sprint fails.
Well: Day 1 standup: “Blocked on the payments API key — need it by tomorrow or I’ll swap to the export task.” The lead unblocks it that afternoon.
The patterns that work: raise blockers EARLY and loudly; write decisions down where the team reads them (channel/wiki, not DMs); over-communicate on async teams (assume nothing was seen); one source of truth for status (the board, not memory); disagreements about code go in review comments with reasons, not opinions.
⚠️ SILENCE IS THE EXPENSIVE OPTION
Every teamwork scenario question has a “said nothing to avoid friction” option — it is always wrong. Early, specific, written communication is always the graded answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

How a team communicates determines how it ships. Verbal-only teams lose context, miss decisions, and burn out. Written-first, async-friendly teams scale and document themselves as a side effect.

Core concepts

1. Written-first. Default to writing things down: design docs, RFCs, decision records, postmortems. Writing forces clarity and creates searchable history.

2. Stand-ups. Daily 15-min check-in: what I did, what I am doing, what is blocking me. Async stand-ups (Slack thread) work well for distributed teams.

3. Async updates. Status updates in Slack, Notion, or email. Avoid meetings where a paragraph would do. Respect timezones and focus time.

4. Synchronous when needed. Some things require real-time: high-bandwidth design discussions, conflict resolution, onboarding. Use video calls for these — text is wrong.

5. Communication across timezones. Document everything. Hand off work explicitly. Avoid 'tag team' models where two people in opposite timezones never overlap.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Decisions made in private 1:1s without writing them up — team loses context.
  • Treating every issue as urgent — Slack pings at 11pm destroy morale.
  • Meetings that should be docs — wastes everyone's time.

Quick recap

Default to writing. Use sync sparingly and well. Async updates respect focus and timezones. Document decisions explicitly.

Glossary

RFC
Request for Comments; a written proposal for technical change.
Postmortem
Written analysis of an incident or project outcome.
Async
Communication that does not require simultaneous presence.

Meeting hygiene: every meeting deserves a clear agenda and a desired OUTCOME — no outcome, no meeting. Clarity check: when unsure you were understood, ask the listener to summarize back what they heard — thirty seconds that prevents a week of rework.

"}, "D687/ch1/s3": {"title": "Conflict, Feedback, and Trust", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Psychological safetyBelief that you will not be punished for speaking up.
Disagree and commitVoicing dissent then supporting the decision once made.
Postmortem cultureBlameless analysis to learn rather than punish.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — a team conflict, de-escalated properly

WORKED EXAMPLE — the framework fight
Two devs deadlock: React vs Vue, and it’s getting personal.
1. Depersonalize — move from “your choice is wrong” to criteria: team experience, hiring pool, project constraints.
2. Evaluate against the criteria — a 30-minute spike each, scored on the agreed criteria.
3. Decide and commit — criteria favor React (3 of 4 teammates know it); the Vue advocate’s concerns get logged as risks to watch. Disagree-and-commit ends it.
Feedback rules that keep trust: specific and behavioral (“the PR sat 4 days”) not personal (“you’re slow”); praise publicly, correct privately; assume good intent. Trust = reliability + honesty over time — the “bank account” every interaction credits or debits.
⚠️ CRITERIA BEFORE CANDIDATES
Agreeing on the DECISION CRITERIA first turns opinion fights into evaluations. That reorder is the correct answer to most conflict scenarios.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Teams without trust cannot ship. Disagreement is healthy; how you handle it is everything. Giving and receiving feedback well is a skill, and it is learnable.

Core concepts

1. Psychological safety. Team members feel safe to speak up, disagree, and be wrong without social punishment. Highest-performing teams (Google research) have it; most do not.

2. Constructive feedback. Specific, actionable, kind. 'Your PR description was unclear about the migration strategy' beats 'Your communication needs work.' Frequent and small beats annual reviews.

3. Receiving feedback. Listen to understand, not to respond. Ask clarifying questions. Thank the giver — they took a risk. Sleep on it before reacting.

4. Resolving technical disagreements. Both share their reasoning. Find shared facts and evidence. Disagree and commit if needed. Escalate to a tiebreaker only if stuck.

5. Recognizing team friction. Decreased participation, snide comments, retros that do not change anything, people quitting. Address it directly; problems do not solve themselves.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Avoiding hard conversations — they get harder the longer you wait.
  • Sandwich feedback (compliment-criticism-compliment) — recipients see through it.
  • Treating disagreement as personal attack — it kills psychological safety.

Quick recap

Trust is built through small interactions over time. Give specific kind feedback often. Receive it gracefully. Resolve disagreements with evidence; escalate only as a last resort.

Glossary

Psychological safety
Belief that you will not be punished for speaking up.
Disagree and commit
Voicing dissent then supporting the decision once made.
Postmortem culture
Blameless analysis to learn rather than punish.

Active listening includes PARAPHRASING what you heard back to the speaker to confirm understanding — “so what I’m hearing is…” It proves attention, surfaces misreads instantly, and de-escalates tension.

📊 FIGURE — red flags in how a team talks
🎯 EXAM TIP
The named red flag for dysfunction is hidden side conversations and triangulation — complaining about a teammate to a third party instead of to them. It corrodes trust and fragments what each person knows, so decisions get made from partial information.
"}, "D687/ch2/s1": {"title": "Scrum Fundamentals", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
SprintA fixed-length development iteration.
VelocityStory points completed per sprint; descriptive, not a target.
Definition of DoneTeam's shared agreement on what 'complete' means.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — one sprint, every Scrum piece in motion

WORKED EXAMPLE — sprint 3 of the team project
• Sprint planning (Mon): from the prioritized backlog, the team pulls stories worth ~20 points into the sprint backlog with a sprint goal: “users can register and log in.”
• Daily standup (15 min): yesterday / today / blockers — sync, not status theater.
• The work: stories move To-Do → In-Progress → Review → Done on the board; the burndown chart tracks remaining points.
• Sprint review (Fri wk2): DEMO working login to stakeholders; feedback becomes new backlog items.
• Retrospective: process, not product — “PRs sat too long; agree on 24-hour review SLA.”
Timeboxes and roles (PO owns backlog, SM owns process, team owns delivery) are what make it Scrum rather than “meetings.”
⚠️ REVIEW ≠ RETRO
Review inspects the PRODUCT (demo, stakeholder feedback). Retrospective inspects the PROCESS (what we change next sprint). The exam swaps them constantly.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Scrum is the most widely adopted Agile framework — and the most widely abused. Knowing how it actually works (vs. how it is often practiced) keeps your team out of common traps.

Core concepts

1. Scrum roles. Product Owner (prioritizes backlog). Scrum Master (facilitates process, removes blockers). Development Team (builds the work). Three roles, distinct responsibilities.

2. Scrum events. Sprint planning (what to build). Daily stand-up (sync, unblock). Sprint review (demo, get feedback). Sprint retrospective (improve process). Each event has a clear purpose.

3. Scrum artifacts. Product backlog (everything the team might do). Sprint backlog (what is in this sprint). Increment (potentially shippable output). Definition of Done.

4. Sprint cadence. Fixed-length iteration (1-4 weeks; 2 most common). At end: demo + retro + plan next. Cadence creates rhythm and predictability.

5. Bad Scrum patterns. Stand-ups that turn into status reports for managers. Sprint goals nobody remembers. Backlog that grows infinitely. Scrum-but: 'we do Scrum but skip retros.' These break the framework.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating velocity as a productivity metric — it games estimation, not real productivity.
  • Stand-ups longer than 15 minutes — usually means the wrong people are in the room.
  • Sprint commitments treated as iron-clad — emergencies happen, adjust.

Quick recap

Scrum has three roles, four events, three artifacts. The cadence is the value. Watch for cargo-culted Scrum — going through motions without the underlying principles.

Glossary

Sprint
A fixed-length development iteration.
Velocity
Story points completed per sprint; descriptive, not a target.
Definition of Done
Team's shared agreement on what 'complete' means.
📊 FIGURE — the three pillars Scrum rests on
🎯 EXAM TIP
Scrum is built on empirical process control, and its three pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. That trio is a common exam item — do not confuse it with the Agile Manifesto's four values or with Scrum's five values (commitment, courage, focus, openness, respect).
"}, "D687/ch2/s2": {"title": "Kanban and Flow-based Work", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
WIPWork In Progress; items currently being worked on.
Lead timeTime from request to delivery.
Cycle timeTime from work start to delivery.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Not all work fits Scrum's sprint cadence. Operational teams, support, content, and continuous-flow product work often do better with Kanban — pull-based, WIP-limited flow.

Core concepts

1. Kanban board. Columns represent workflow stages (Backlog → In Progress → Review → Done). Cards move left to right. Visualizes flow and bottlenecks.

2. WIP limits. Cap how many items can be in any stage at once. Forces focus, exposes bottlenecks. Often the single highest-leverage Kanban practice.

3. Flow metrics. Lead time (idea → done). Cycle time (work started → done). Throughput (items per week). Trend these over time.

4. Pull vs push. In Kanban, work is pulled by capacity, not pushed by deadlines. When a slot opens up, the next item comes in. Different mindset from Scrum.

5. Kanban vs Scrum. Scrum: time-boxed, planning ceremonies, sprint commitment. Kanban: continuous flow, WIP-limited, fewer ceremonies. Many teams use a hybrid (Scrumban).

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • No WIP limits — Kanban becomes 'a board with sticky notes.'
  • Ignoring cycle time — slow flow is invisible without metrics.
  • Mixing project and operational work without separating swim lanes — chaos.

Quick recap

Kanban is pull-based, WIP-limited, continuous flow. Visualize work, limit work-in-progress, measure flow. Choose Kanban when work is steady-state or operational; Scrum when iterative product development.

Glossary

WIP
Work In Progress; items currently being worked on.
Lead time
Time from request to delivery.
Cycle time
Time from work start to delivery.

Cycle time measures the time work is ACTIVELY being done from start to finish — the flow metric teams can most directly improve. Bottlenecks reveal themselves on the board as cards piling up BEFORE a stage — the queue in front of the constraint.

"}, "D687/ch2/s3": {"title": "User Stories and Backlog Refinement", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
User storyShort description of a feature from a user perspective.
INVESTMnemonic for what makes a good story.
Acceptance criteriaExplicit conditions for a story to be considered done.
Spot the weak story“Add stuff to website” fails every test — no user, no goal, no benefit, unestimable.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — writing a story that’s actually ready

WORKED EXAMPLE — from vague wish to sprint-ready story
• ❌ “Add search.”
• ✅ “As a returning customer, I want to search orders by product name so that I can reorder quickly.”
Acceptance criteria (testable!): matching orders listed newest-first; no-results state shows suggestions; results within 2s.
INVEST check: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small (fits a sprint — if not, SPLIT: search-by-name now, filters later), Testable.
Refinement: the team estimates it (5 points), asks the PO questions, and only DEFINED-and-estimated stories enter sprint planning. Epic → stories → tasks is the decomposition ladder.
⚠️ ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA = THE TESTS IN PROSE
A story without testable criteria can’t be verified “done.” The as-a/I-want/so-that format plus criteria is the graded template — options missing the WHY (“so that”) are incomplete.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Bad stories cause bad sprints. A vague 'add login' story leads to scope creep, missed edge cases, and rework. Good stories enable predictable, incremental delivery.

Core concepts

1. User story format. 'As a [user], I want [goal], so that [reason].' Forces you to articulate who, what, why. Avoid stories that are pure tech tasks ('refactor X') — those are tasks, not stories.

2. INVEST criteria. Independent (no story-to-story dependencies). Negotiable (not a contract). Valuable (delivers value). Estimable (can be sized). Small (fits in a sprint). Testable (clear pass/fail).

3. Acceptance criteria. Specific conditions that must hold for the story to be 'done.' 'Login form rejects passwords under 8 chars with error message X.' Removes ambiguity.

4. Estimation. Story points: relative size, not time. Fibonacci scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8). T-shirt sizes (S/M/L/XL) for early-stage. Estimate as a team for shared understanding.

5. Backlog refinement. Regular session to clarify, split, estimate, and prioritize upcoming stories. Keeps top of backlog ready for sprint planning. Often weekly, ~1 hour.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Stories that are too big to finish in a sprint — split them.
  • Acceptance criteria written by one person, never reviewed — misses cases.
  • Estimating in hours instead of points — invites schedule pressure and gaming.

Quick recap

User stories with clear acceptance criteria are the unit of work. Apply INVEST, refine continuously, estimate as a team. Better stories produce better sprints.

Glossary

User story
Short description of a feature from a user perspective.
INVEST
Mnemonic for what makes a good story.
Acceptance criteria
Explicit conditions for a story to be considered done.

Spot the weak story: “Add stuff to website” fails every test — no user, no goal, no benefit, unestimable. The classic format is: As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit] — the benefit clause is what makes prioritization possible. The Product Owner ultimately owns story content and prioritization; the team owns estimates and how.

"}, "D687/ch2/s4": {"title": "Sprint Reviews and Retrospectives", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Sprint reviewDemo of completed work to stakeholders at sprint end.
RetrospectiveTeam meeting to inspect process and improve.
BlamelessFocused on systems and learning, not individual blame.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — a retrospective that changes something

WORKED EXAMPLE — the retro after a rough sprint
Sprint 3 delivered 12 of 20 points. The retro (safe space, blameless):
• What went well: pairing on the auth bug; CI caught two breaks.
• What didn’t: two stories were under-specified mid-sprint; PRs waited 3+ days.
• Five whys on the PR delays: reviews felt optional → no agreed SLA → busy people deferred.
• Action items (owned + checkable): 24-hour review SLA (owner: lead, check next retro); stories enter planning only with acceptance criteria (owner: PO).
Next retro opens by CHECKING those actions — that follow-through is what separates continuous improvement from a venting session.
⚠️ NO OWNED ACTIONS = NO RETRO
The graded answer shape: retros produce a small number of SPECIFIC, OWNED, FOLLOWED-UP process changes. “We discussed feelings” is the distractor.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most teams run reviews and retros mechanically and gain nothing from them. Run them well and they become the engine of team improvement.

Core concepts

1. Sprint review goal. Demo working software to stakeholders. Get feedback on what was built. Adjust the backlog based on what was learned. Not a status meeting.

2. Demo discipline. Show working software, not slides. Walk through user flows, not implementation. Capture feedback live. Schedule follow-ups for things that need design.

3. Retrospective format. What went well, what did not, what to try. Keep it blameless. Vote on action items. Pick 1-3 to commit to. Track them next retro.

4. Action items that stick. Specific, owned, and small. 'We will pair-program PRs over 500 lines for the next sprint' beats 'We will collaborate more.' Owners get held accountable.

5. Anti-patterns. Retro that surfaces same issue every sprint without action. Retro skipped because 'busy.' Retro turned into a venting session with no improvements. All kill momentum.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Skipping retros when sprints go well — that is when you can experiment safely.
  • Action items that nobody owns or tracks — they die.
  • Letting one person dominate the retro — get everyone speaking.

Quick recap

Reviews demo working software and get stakeholder feedback. Retros surface what to change. Both produce small, committed, owned actions that get tracked.

Glossary

Sprint review
Demo of completed work to stakeholders at sprint end.
Retrospective
Team meeting to inspect process and improve.
Blameless
Focused on systems and learning, not individual blame.
📊 FIGURE — reviving a retro that has become a ritual
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Reading a quiet retrospective as "nothing is wrong". A retro that has become a mute ritual is usually signalling low psychological safety, not a healthy team. Fix it by changing the format, rotating who facilitates, and dealing with safety directly — and by actually shipping at least one improvement so people see that speaking up changes something.
"}, "D687/ch3/s1": {"title": "Branching Strategies (GitFlow, Trunk-based)", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
TrunkMain development branch (often called main or master).
Feature flagRuntime toggle for enabling/disabling features.
HotfixUrgent fix branched from production.
Branch naming disciplinemixed conventions like feat/x, feature-y, and z-fix cause confusion and BREAK AUTOMATION — CI rules, changelog generators, and branch policies all key off consistent prefixes.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — choosing a branching strategy for the team

WORKED EXAMPLE — GitFlow vs trunk-based for a 5-person team
• GitFlow: long-lived develop + feature/release/hotfix branches — structure for versioned releases, but branches drift and merges get painful.
• Trunk-based: short-lived branches (a day or two) merged to main constantly behind CI — small merges, always-releasable main; requires discipline + good tests (+ feature flags for unfinished work).
For a capstone team shipping continuously: trunk-based with short feature branches + PR review is the usual right answer. The rule that matters most either way: branches live SHORT — merge pain grows with divergence time.
⚠️ LONG-LIVED BRANCHES = MERGE DEBT
“Why did the two-week feature branch explode on merge?” → main moved on; divergence compounds. Small, frequent merges are the graded principle across every strategy question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

How your team uses branches shapes how often you ship and how painful merges are. Pick the wrong strategy and every release becomes a rescue mission.

Core concepts

1. GitFlow. Long-lived develop and main branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches. Heavy ceremony. Useful for versioned releases (mobile apps, libraries).

2. GitHub Flow. Single main branch. Branch off, PR, merge to main. Simple, fast. Best for web apps with continuous deploy.

3. Trunk-based development. Everyone commits to (or near) main. Tiny, frequent merges. Feature flags for incomplete work. Fastest for high-velocity teams; requires strong testing.

4. Choosing strategy. Mobile apps with versioned releases: GitFlow. Web apps shipping daily: GitHub Flow or trunk-based. Strong CI/CD: trunk-based wins on velocity.

5. Avoiding merge hell. Merge frequently (rebase or merge from main daily). Keep branches short-lived (under 3 days). Coordinate large refactors. Resist long-running side branches.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Long-lived feature branches that drift from main — merging is painful and bug-prone.
  • Adopting GitFlow for a fast-moving web app — overkill, slows everyone down.
  • Trunk-based without feature flags — half-built features ship to users.

Quick recap

GitFlow for versioned releases. GitHub Flow for simple cases. Trunk-based for max velocity. Match strategy to your release cadence and CI maturity.

Glossary

Trunk
Main development branch (often called main or master).
Feature flag
Runtime toggle for enabling/disabling features.
Hotfix
Urgent fix branched from production.

Branch naming discipline: mixed conventions like feat/x, feature-y, and z-fix cause confusion and BREAK AUTOMATION — CI rules, changelog generators, and branch policies all key off consistent prefixes. Pick one convention; enforce it.

"}, "D687/ch3/s2": {"title": "Pull Requests and Code Review", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
PRPull Request; proposed code change for review and merge.
ReviewerEngineer who reviews and approves/rejects a PR.
SquashCombining multiple commits into one before merge.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — a pull request that gets approved fast

WORKED EXAMPLE — anatomy of a good PR + a good review
The PR: small (≈200 lines, one concern), titled “Add order search endpoint,” description says WHAT + WHY + how to test, links the story, CI green before requesting review.
The review: reviewer checks correctness, tests, readability — comments are specific and kind: “This loop re-queries per item — could we batch? (n+1 pattern)” not “this is bad.” Blocking issues vs nitpicks labeled (“nit:”). Author responds to every comment (fix or reasoned pushback), re-requests review.
Approval + squash-merge keeps history clean. Review is knowledge-sharing as much as defect-catching — the second pair of eyes that also spreads context.
⚠️ BIG PRs GET RUBBER-STAMPED
A 2,000-line PR gets “LGTM” because nobody can actually review it — small PRs get REAL review. “What improves review quality most?” → smaller changes, every time.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Code review is where bugs are caught, knowledge spreads, and team standards get enforced. Done well, it accelerates teams. Done poorly, it bottlenecks them.

Core concepts

1. Good PR descriptions. What, why, how. Link issue. List testing done. Note reviewable size. Reviewers should not have to guess your intent.

2. PR size. Smaller is better — under 400 lines is the sweet spot. Big PRs get rubber-stamped or rejected. Split large changes into chained PRs.

3. Review checklist. Does it solve the right problem? Are tests adequate? Edge cases handled? Does it follow conventions? Security implications? Performance reasonable?

4. Constructive review feedback. Specific. Suggest, do not demand (unless required). Distinguish 'must-fix' from 'nice-to-have.' Praise good code; teach when reviewing junior engineers.

5. Resolving feedback efficiently. Address every comment, even if just to acknowledge. Push fixes as separate commits during review (squash later). Re-request review when ready.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • PRs over 1000 lines — reviewers cannot do their job; merging them is a guess.
  • Pedantic style nitpicks dominating reviews — automate style with a formatter.
  • Author getting defensive about feedback — kills review culture.

Quick recap

Small, well-described PRs with good tests get reviewed quickly and merged cleanly. Reviewers focus on correctness, design, and tests; let the linter handle style.

Glossary

PR
Pull Request; proposed code change for review and merge.
Reviewer
Engineer who reviews and approves/rejects a PR.
Squash
Combining multiple commits into one before merge.

A great PR description answers three things: WHAT changed and WHY, HOW to test it, and screenshots when UI changed. Reviewers who can see intent and verification path review faster and better.

"}, "D687/ch3/s3": {"title": "Merge Conflicts and Resolution", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Conflict markerGit markers showing competing versions in a file.
RebaseReapplying commits onto a different base commit.
reflogGit's log of local reference changes; lets you recover lost commits.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — a team merge conflict, resolved calmly

WORKED EXAMPLE — both of you edited PriceCalculator
You merge main into your branch and Git stops:
<<<<<<< HEAD (yours)
  return subtotal * 0.9;      // your 10% discount
=======
  return subtotal + shipping;  // teammate's shipping change
>>>>>>> main
The conflict is Git saying “same lines, two intents — a HUMAN must decide.” Correct resolution usually means UNDERSTANDING both intents, often combining: return (subtotal + shipping) * 0.9; — and when intents genuinely clash, a 5-minute conversation with the teammate beats guessing. Then: remove markers, run the tests, commit the merge.
Prevention: pull main often, keep branches short, coordinate on hot files.
⚠️ NEVER PICK A SIDE BLIND
“Accept yours” wholesale deletes a teammate’s work silently. The graded behavior: read both changes, preserve both intents (or talk), test before committing.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Merge conflicts happen. The skill is not avoiding them — it is resolving them confidently and not breaking main. Bad conflict resolution causes silent bugs that survive code review.

Core concepts

1. What conflicts are. Two branches changed the same lines. Git cannot choose; you must. Conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) show competing versions.

2. Resolving conflicts. Open the file, choose what to keep (often a combination). Remove markers. Test that both sides' intent is preserved. Commit.

3. Rebase vs merge. Merge: combine branches with a merge commit; preserves history. Rebase: replay commits onto target; linear history but rewrites commits. Choose by team convention.

4. Frequent rebase or merge. Pull from main daily. Small conflicts are easy; week-old conflicts are hell. This is the single biggest defense against merge pain.

5. Recovering from bad merges. git reflog shows your local history. git reset --hard reverts. git revert creates an inverse commit. Backups (push to a personal branch) before risky operations.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Resolving by accepting one side blindly — silent loss of work.
  • Force-pushing to shared branches — overwrites others' commits.
  • Skipping tests after a merge — the conflict resolution itself can introduce bugs.

Quick recap

Conflicts are normal. Resolve carefully, preserving both sides' intent. Choose rebase or merge by team standard. Pull frequently to keep conflicts small.

Glossary

Conflict marker
Git markers showing competing versions in a file.
Rebase
Reapplying commits onto a different base commit.
reflog
Git's log of local reference changes; lets you recover lost commits.
📊 FIGURE — reuse recorded resolution
🎯 EXAM TIP
git rerere stands for reuse recorded resolution: it remembers how you settled a conflict and replays that resolution automatically when the identical conflict shows up again. It earns its keep on a long-running branch you rebase over and over, where you would otherwise resolve the same collision every time.
"}, "D687/ch3/s4": {"title": "Tagging, Releases, and Hotfixes", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
SemverSemantic Versioning convention.
TagPointer to a specific commit, used for marking releases.
BackportApplying a fix made on a release branch to the main branch.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — tagging a release and shipping a hotfix

WORKED EXAMPLE — v1.2.0 ships, then breaks
Release: git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Search + export"; push tags; the tag pins EXACTLY what shipped (semantic versioning: MAJOR breaking / MINOR features / PATCH fixes).
Tuesday: production bug in v1.2.0 while main already has unfinished v1.3 work. Hotfix flow: branch FROM THE TAG (git checkout -b hotfix/1.2.1 v1.2.0) → fix → test → tag v1.2.1 → deploy → merge the hotfix back into main so the fix isn’t lost in v1.3.
That last merge-back is the step teams forget — and the bug “returns” in the next release.
⚠️ HOTFIX FROM THE TAG, NOT FROM MAIN
Branching the fix from main would ship unfinished v1.3 work to production. Branch from the released tag; merge back to main after. Both directions are exam-tested.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Releases are a coordination problem as much as a technical one. Versioning, tagging, and hotfix workflows let teams ship reliably and recover fast when things break.

Core concepts

1. Semantic versioning. MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increment MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for fixes. Industry standard for libraries and APIs.

2. Git tags. Lightweight pointers to specific commits. Tag releases (v1.2.3). Use annotated tags for releases — they carry metadata.

3. Release process. Cut release branch (or tag from main). Run release tests. Deploy to staging. Deploy to production with monitoring. Document changes (changelog).

4. Hotfix workflow. Branch from production tag. Fix. Test. Deploy. Backport fix to main. Document in changelog. Schedule a postmortem if it was a serious bug.

5. Coordinating cross-team releases. Stage gates. Compatibility matrices. Feature flags for staged rollouts. Communication channel for the launch window. Rollback plan ready before launch.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting to backport hotfixes to main — same bug returns next release.
  • Versioning that does not follow semver — consumers cannot reason about safety.
  • No rollback plan — when production breaks at 3am, you are improvising.

Quick recap

Use semantic versioning. Tag releases. Define a release process and follow it. Hotfixes branch from production and backport. Always have a rollback plan.

Glossary

Semver
Semantic Versioning convention.
Tag
Pointer to a specific commit, used for marking releases.
Backport
Applying a fix made on a release branch to the main branch.
"}, "D687/ch4/s1": {"title": "Code Style and Linting", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
LinterTool that flags likely bugs and style issues statically.
FormatterTool that rewrites code to a consistent style.
Pre-commitHook that runs checks before allowing a git commit.
Naminga descriptive identifier reveals intent everywhere it appears — elapsedDays beats d. If a name needs a comment to explain it, rename it.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

📖 Worked example — style & linting as team policy

WORKED EXAMPLE — ending the tabs-vs-spaces war forever
Sprint 1’s PRs are full of formatting nitpicks. The fix is POLICY-AS-TOOLING:
1. Adopt a standard style (language-standard defaults) — the choice matters less than having one.
2. Auto-formatter (Prettier/Black/google-java-format) runs on save — formatting debates end.
3. Linter (ESLint/Checkstyle/pylint) catches BUGS-in-waiting: unused vars, == vs ===, unreachable code.
4. Enforce in CI + pre-commit hooks — violations fail the build, so no human polices style.
Result: review comments drop from 30 nitpicks to 4 substantive points — reviewers now review LOGIC. Consistency beats preference; automation beats vigilance.
⚠️ FORMATTER ≠ LINTER
Formatter rewrites layout (spacing/wrapping); linter flags suspicious CODE (potential bugs, smells). “Which catches the unused variable?” → the linter. Exams test the split.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Style debates kill review cycles. Automate them and reviews focus on what matters: correctness, design, and tests.

Core concepts

1. Linters. Static analysis for likely bugs and style violations. Python: flake8, pylint, ruff. JS/TS: eslint. Run in CI; block PRs that fail.

2. Formatters. Auto-format code to a consistent style. Python: black, ruff format. JS/TS: prettier. Removes style debates entirely — accept the formatter's output.

3. Pre-commit hooks. Run linter and formatter before commit. Tools: pre-commit (Python), husky (JS). Catches issues before they hit CI.

4. What to enforce vs suggest. Enforce: anything that can break production (unused imports, syntax errors, security issues). Suggest: style preferences. Automate the former.

5. Editor integration. VSCode, IntelliJ, etc. show lint warnings live. Saves debug cycles. Standard part of modern dev environment setup.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Bikeshedding style — accept the formatter and move on.
  • Linter rules so strict nothing passes — pragmatic config wins.
  • Pre-commit hooks that take 30 seconds — devs disable them.

Quick recap

Automate style and basic correctness. Linters block bugs; formatters end debates. Pre-commit hooks catch issues early. Editor integration makes the loop tight.

Glossary

Linter
Tool that flags likely bugs and style issues statically.
Formatter
Tool that rewrites code to a consistent style.
Pre-commit
Hook that runs checks before allowing a git commit.

📘 Deep dive: code style & linting

A linter performs static analysis — it reads code WITHOUT running it and flags bugs, smells, and style violations (ESLint, Pylint). A formatter (Prettier, Black) rewrites code to a canonical layout so humans stop debating tabs. A style guide makes a large team’s code read like one author wrote it — lower review friction, faster onboarding. Run linting in the CI pipeline so violations fail the build before review, not after.

Naming: a descriptive identifier reveals intent everywhere it appears — elapsedDays beats d. If a name needs a comment to explain it, rename it.

"}, "D687/ch4/s2": {"title": "Unit, Integration, and E2E Testing", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
MockStand-in object that simulates a dependency.
Flaky testTest that fails intermittently without code changes.
Test fixtureSetup data or state for tests.
Test datause fixtures and factories to create small, controlled data — never point tests at production.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

📖 Worked example — the test pyramid on one feature

WORKED EXAMPLE — testing “checkout” at three levels
• Unit (many, milliseconds): calcTotal([item(2, 9.99)]) returns 19.98; tax edge cases; empty-cart case.
• Integration (some): OrderService + real test DB — order persists, stock decrements atomically.
• E2E (few, minutes): a headless browser adds an item, checks out, sees the confirmation — the whole stack, exactly like a user.
The pyramid shape is the point: MANY fast units → SOME integrations → FEW E2E. Inverted pyramids (all E2E) are slow, flaky, and vague about what broke; units pinpoint failures instantly.
⚠️ E2E FAILURES DON’T LOCALIZE
An E2E red says “something broke somewhere”; a unit red names the function. That diagnostic difference is WHY the pyramid is bottom-heavy — the reasoning exams ask for.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tests are how teams move fast without breaking things. The right balance of unit, integration, and end-to-end tests gives you confidence at each level.

Core concepts

1. Test pyramid. Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests. Inversion (mostly E2E) is slow and flaky.

2. Unit tests. Test one function or class in isolation. Fast (milliseconds). Mock dependencies. Should make up the bulk of your suite.

3. Integration tests. Test components working together (with database, with API). Slower but catch interaction bugs. Run on every PR.

4. E2E tests. Test full user flows through the real (or near-real) system. Slowest, most realistic. Run on PRs to main only.

5. Avoiding flaky tests. Tests that fail intermittently. Causes: timing assumptions, shared state, network calls. Quarantine flaky tests; fix or delete them.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Mocking so heavily that tests pass while the real code is broken.
  • E2E tests for everything — slow CI, flaky failures, low confidence.
  • Tests coupled to implementation details — every refactor breaks them.

Quick recap

Balance unit, integration, and E2E. Aim for a pyramid shape: fast feedback at the bottom, realistic checks at the top. Fix flaky tests aggressively.

Glossary

Mock
Stand-in object that simulates a dependency.
Flaky test
Test that fails intermittently without code changes.
Test fixture
Setup data or state for tests.

📘 Deep dive: the testing pyramid, determinism & coverage

Pyramid: many fast unit tests (each tests one piece in isolation, dependencies replaced by test doubles/mocks), fewer integration tests (pieces together), fewest end-to-end tests (whole system, slowest). Deterministic tests produce the same result every run; a test that passes and fails non-deterministically is flaky — the purpose of isolation is determinism. Code coverage measures the percentage of code executed by tests — useful signal, but 100% coverage does not prove correctness; it only proves execution.

Test data: use fixtures and factories to create small, controlled data — never point tests at production. Test names describe the expected behavior under specific conditions. Structure: Arrange–Act–Assert — set up, do the thing, check the result. Snapshot tests compare output against a stored version; update the snapshot deliberately when behavior legitimately changes — never blindly.

"}, "D687/ch4/s3": {"title": "CI Pipelines and Build Automation", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
CIContinuous Integration; automated checks on every change.
PipelineSequence of jobs that run in CI.
Branch protectionRepo rules requiring CI/approvals before merge.
Secrets (API keys, passwords)injected at runtime from a secret manager — never committed to the repo.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Continuous Integration runs tests, lints, and builds on every PR — catching problems before they reach main. Without CI, every merge is a roll of the dice.

Core concepts

1. CI fundamentals. On every push or PR, run: install deps, lint, test, build. Fail fast on errors. Block merge if CI fails.

2. Tools. GitHub Actions (most common in modern teams). GitLab CI. Jenkins (legacy but powerful). CircleCI. All have YAML-defined workflows.

3. Branch protection. Require CI green and N approvals before merge to main. Configured at the repo level. Non-negotiable for any team.

4. Optimizing CI runtime. Cache dependencies, parallelize tests, run only changed scopes. Aim for under 10 minutes total. Slow CI strangles velocity.

5. Handling CI failures. Read the log. Reproduce locally if possible. If flaky, retry once and quarantine if it recurs. Do not merge with red CI; never disable failing tests to merge.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Disabling tests to make CI green — accumulating debt and silent bugs.
  • CI that takes 30+ minutes — devs work around it, not with it.
  • No branch protection — accidents happen, and they are often public.

Quick recap

CI on every PR with branch protection is the floor for serious teams. Keep it fast, treat failures seriously, and never bypass it.

Glossary

CI
Continuous Integration; automated checks on every change.
Pipeline
Sequence of jobs that run in CI.
Branch protection
Repo rules requiring CI/approvals before merge.

📘 Deep dive: CI pipelines & build artifacts

Typical pipeline stages: build → test → package → deploy, defined as pipeline-as-code in the repo. A build artifact is the packaged output (JAR, container image) produced once and promoted through environments — never rebuilt per environment. Caching dependencies between runs and parallelizing test suites are the two standard levers that cut pipeline time. Defining pipelines in code reduces “works on my machine” drift and makes the process reviewable.

Secrets (API keys, passwords) are injected at runtime from a secret manager — never committed to the repo. Self-hosted runners are useful when builds need special hardware or a private network. Test selection runs only the tests affected by a change to keep feedback fast.

"}, "D687/ch4/s4": {"title": "Code Review at Scale", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
CODEOWNERSGitHub file mapping paths to maintainer accounts.
SLAService Level Agreement; expected turnaround.
BikesheddingDisproportionate debate over trivial decisions.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

📖 Worked example — keeping reviews fast as the team grows

WORKED EXAMPLE — review SLAs, ownership, and load balancing
Six devs, PRs piling up. The working system:
• SLA: first review within 24h (retro-agreed, tracked).
• CODEOWNERS: payment paths auto-request the payments-savvy reviewer — expertise routing.
• Load balancing: rotate default reviewers so one senior isn’t the bottleneck (and juniors grow by reviewing).
• Author prep: small PRs, self-review first, CI green, description with test steps — respect reviewer time.
• Automation first: formatters/linters/tests comment automatically; humans review design and correctness only.
Review debt compounds like merge debt — the system, not heroics, keeps it flowing.
⚠️ THE BOTTLENECK IS USUALLY PROCESS, NOT PEOPLE
“Reviews are slow — what first?” → smaller PRs + agreed SLA + automated checks, not “review faster.” Systemic answers over personal ones, every time.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

On a 5-person team, anyone can review anything. On a 50-person team, review needs structure or it becomes a bottleneck or rubber stamp.

Core concepts

1. Review SLAs. Team agreement: PRs reviewed within X hours. Without SLAs, PRs sit, authors lose context, throughput drops.

2. Distributing review load. Use codeowners files (GitHub auto-assigns). Rotate reviewers. Avoid one senior reviewing everything — they burn out.

3. CODEOWNERS. Map paths to maintainers. Ensures the right experts review changes. Auto-assigned by GitHub.

4. Avoiding bikeshedding. Trivial disagreements (variable names, style) consume disproportionate time. Use the formatter; for true preferences, defer to author.

5. Review culture. Praise good code. Distinguish must-fix from nit. Be kind to junior engineers (their first PR sets the tone). Review like you want to be reviewed.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Senior engineer reviews everything — single point of failure and bottleneck.
  • Reviewers who only nitpick — produce slow, demoralized teams.
  • PRs sitting for days — context lost, author loses motivation.

Quick recap

Review SLAs, distributed load via codeowners, kind and substantive feedback. Scale review by structure, not by adding more senior reviewers.

Glossary

CODEOWNERS
GitHub file mapping paths to maintainer accounts.
SLA
Service Level Agreement; expected turnaround.
Bikeshedding
Disproportionate debate over trivial decisions.

📘 Deep dive: code review at scale

Keep pull requests small and single-purpose — review quality collapses past a few hundred lines. Let automation go first: linting, tests, and coverage run before a human looks, so reviewers spend attention on design and correctness. Distinguish blocking issues (bugs, security, broken contracts) from nits (naming, style preferences) and label them. Review the CODE, not the coder — comments name problems and suggest alternatives.

"}, "D687/ch5/s1": {"title": "Requirements Gathering and Specs", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
RequirementStated need the system must satisfy.
SpecWritten description of what is being built.
Scope creepGradual expansion of work without explicit approval.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

📖 Worked example — from stakeholder interview to spec

WORKED EXAMPLE — “we need a dashboard” becomes requirements
Interview the sponsor with open questions: WHO uses it (support agents), for WHAT decision (spot ticket backlogs), how CURRENT (5-min refresh is fine), on what (desktop).
Write it down as:
• Functional: “display open-ticket count per queue, refreshed ≤ 5 min; filter by priority.”
• Non-functional: loads < 3s; read-only role required.
• Out of scope: mobile app, historical analytics (v2).
Then confirm back: walk the spec with the stakeholder, capture sign-off. Requirements churn later is normal — change control (impact → approve → re-baseline) keeps it sane. The spec is the team’s contract AND the acceptance test list.
⚠️ THE FIRST ANSWER IS NEVER THE REQUIREMENT
Stakeholders name solutions (“a dashboard”); asking WHY twice surfaces the need (spot backlogs fast). Requirement = the need + measurable criteria, not the first artifact named.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

More software is built that solves the wrong problem than is built poorly. Good requirements work surfaces the actual problem before code is written.

Core concepts

1. Stakeholder interviews. Talk to the people who will use the software. Ask 'what are you trying to do' before 'what features do you want.' Requirements emerge; they are not handed over.

2. Functional requirements. What the system does. 'Users can log in with email and password.' Testable.

3. Non-functional requirements. How well it does it: performance (under 200ms), availability (99.9%), security, accessibility, scalability. Often ignored until they bite you.

4. Spec documents. Written description of what is being built. Shared with stakeholders for sign-off. Reduces 'that is not what I meant' rework.

5. Avoiding scope creep. Use the spec as the contract. New asks go to the next iteration. Document explicitly when scope changes.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Skipping interviews and assuming you know — you usually do not.
  • Writing specs nobody reads — keep them short, focus on what matters.
  • Saying yes to every new feature mid-sprint — death by a thousand cuts.

Quick recap

Talk to users. Capture functional and non-functional requirements. Write a spec, get sign-off, and use it to defend scope. Iterate explicitly.

Glossary

Requirement
Stated need the system must satisfy.
Spec
Written description of what is being built.
Scope creep
Gradual expansion of work without explicit approval.

📘 Deep dive: requirements gathering

Functional requirements describe what the system DOES (behaviors); non-functional requirements describe qualities — performance, security, availability, usability. Elicitation techniques: stakeholder interviews, observation of real work, document analysis, prototypes. Write user stories (“As a … I want … so that …”) with acceptance criteria that make “done” testable. The costliest defects are ambiguous requirements discovered late — precision here is cheaper than rework.

A requirements document primarily captures WHAT to build and why — only as much documentation as is needed, and no longer. MoSCoW prioritization: Must have, Should have, Could have, Will-not have (this time). It is a living document — it evolves with learnings rather than being locked. Personas are fictional archetypal users that anchor decisions; they complement, never replace, contact with real users.

"}, "D687/ch5/s2": {"title": "Estimation and Planning", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Story pointRelative effort estimate.
VelocityStory points completed per sprint, averaged.
Brooks' Law'Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.'
Time-boxing risk researchallocate a FIXED amount of time to investigate an unknown, then decide with what you learned — momentum beats perfect information.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — planning a sprint with story points

WORKED EXAMPLE — velocity math + planning poker
Planning poker on “order search”: votes 3, 5, 5, 13 → the 13 explains (“search needs an index migration”) → discussion → re-vote converges on 8. The outlier conversation IS the value: it surfaced hidden work.
Velocity: last three sprints delivered 19, 23, 21 points → plan ~21 for next sprint. The team pulls stories totaling 20 — not 30, however optimistic anyone feels.
Points are RELATIVE size (complexity+effort+uncertainty, Fibonacci scale), not hours — comparing to reference stories beats absolute guessing, and velocity converts points to schedule honestly.
⚠️ VELOCITY IS A MEASURE, NOT A TARGET
Inflating estimates to “raise velocity” or management using velocity to compare teams corrupts the signal. It forecasts capacity; it isn’t a performance grade — the ethics-of-metrics answer exams look for.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Software estimation is famously bad — projects routinely take 2-3x what teams predicted. Knowing why, and how to plan around it, separates predictable teams from chronically late ones.

Core concepts

1. Story points. Relative size estimates (Fibonacci: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13). Avoid time-based estimates that get confused with deadlines. Estimate as a team for shared mental model.

2. T-shirt sizing. S/M/L/XL for early-stage estimates when details are unclear. Faster than story points, less precise. Useful for roadmapping.

3. Estimation biases. Optimism bias (we underestimate). Anchoring (first number proposed dominates). Planning fallacy (we forget complications). All push estimates too low.

4. Sprint planning. Pull as much from backlog as fits the team's velocity. Commit to a sprint goal — even if details slip, the goal should be hit.

5. Adjusting plans to reality. When things slip, decide: cut scope, push deadline, add people (rarely helps short-term), or compromise quality. All have costs; pick deliberately.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating estimates as commitments — destroys honesty in estimation.
  • Adding people to a late project (Brooks' Law) — usually makes it later.
  • Not adjusting plans when reality diverges — leads to demoralizing death marches.

Quick recap

Estimate relatively (story points, t-shirt sizes). Know your biases. Plan with velocity but stay honest. Adjust scope, deadline, or quality explicitly when reality changes.

Glossary

Story point
Relative effort estimate.
Velocity
Story points completed per sprint, averaged.
Brooks' Law
'Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.'

Time-boxing risk research: allocate a FIXED amount of time to investigate an unknown, then decide with what you learned — momentum beats perfect information. And re-estimating large items as you learn is normal and helpful — estimates are forecasts, not promises.

"}, "D687/ch5/s3": {"title": "Risk and Dependency Management", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Risk registerStructured list of project risks and mitigations.
DependencyExternal entity your project relies on for success.
MitigationAction taken to reduce risk likelihood or impact.
Tech debt as riskit COMPOUNDS — slowing delivery and raising outage risk the longer it sits.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — a risk register that actually gets used

WORKED EXAMPLE — four risks, scored and answered
Risk                        P    Impact  Score  Response
Payment API sandbox flaky   H    H       9      MITIGATE: mock fallback + retry
Only Dana knows deployment  M    H       6      MITIGATE: pair + runbook
Scope creep from sponsor    H    M       6      MITIGATE: change control
Cloud free tier expires     L    H       3      TRANSFER/ACCEPT: budget alert
Score = probability × impact ranks attention. The four responses: avoid (change the plan), mitigate (reduce P or impact), transfer (insure/outsource), accept (watch). Dependencies get the same treatment: the critical path (DB schema → API → UI) is where slips cascade — track blockers ON that path hardest, and revisit the register at every sprint boundary.
⚠️ A RISK OWNED BY NOBODY IS ACCEPTED BY ACCIDENT
Each register row needs an owner and a trigger/checkpoint. “We listed risks in week 1” then never re-read = the classic capstone failure scenario.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The bugs that kill projects are usually predictable risks ignored early. Surfacing them, owning them, and mitigating actively is the difference between a smooth project and a fire drill.

Core concepts

1. Risk identification. List what could go wrong. Technical (a key library is unstable), team (key person leaves), external (vendor changes API). Brainstorm with the team.

2. Risk register. Track each risk: description, likelihood, impact, mitigation, owner. Review weekly. Closed risks are removed; new ones added.

3. Dependency mapping. Identify external teams, services, vendors, or other projects you rely on. Communicate early. Build buffer time.

4. Mitigation strategies. Avoid (change plan to remove risk), reduce (probability or impact), transfer (contracts, insurance), accept (with explicit approval).

5. Communicating to leadership. Surface real risks early — leadership cannot help if they only hear good news. Be specific about likelihood and impact.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Hiding risks because raising them feels negative — they always emerge later, worse.
  • Risk register that is created once and never updated — useless.
  • Believing 'X team will deliver on time' without verification — they often will not.

Quick recap

Identify risks early, track them in a register, assign owners, mitigate actively. Communicate clearly to leadership. Dependencies are risks too.

Glossary

Risk register
Structured list of project risks and mitigations.
Dependency
External entity your project relies on for success.
Mitigation
Action taken to reduce risk likelihood or impact.

Tech debt as risk: it COMPOUNDS — slowing delivery and raising outage risk the longer it sits. An SPOF (single point of failure) is a component whose failure halts the entire system — find them, add redundancy or a fallback.

"}, "D687/ch5/s4": {"title": "Shipping and Post-Launch", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
CanarySmall initial deploy to detect issues before full rollout.
PostmortemBlameless written analysis of an incident.
SLOService Level Objective; target metric like 99.9% uptime.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Launch is not the end — it is the beginning of the next phase. Teams that have explicit go/no-go criteria, monitor on-call, and respond to incidents calmly ship better software, longer.

Core concepts

1. Go/no-go criteria. Specific conditions to launch: tests green, key metrics in range, monitoring set up, rollback tested. Document them before the launch window.

2. Production launches. Stage rollout (canary → 1% → 10% → 100%). Watch metrics at each stage. Rollback path tested. Communication channel open during launch window.

3. Post-launch monitoring. Track key metrics: error rates, latency, user-facing metrics (signup rate, conversion). Compare to pre-launch baseline. Alert on regressions.

4. Incident response. Page → diagnose → mitigate → resolve → write postmortem. Mitigation often differs from full fix. Restore service first, fix root cause after.

5. Postmortems. Blameless analysis of what happened, why, and how to prevent. Output: action items with owners. Read postmortems from other teams to learn.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Launching on Friday afternoon — bugs surface over the weekend with skeleton crew.
  • Skipping postmortems for 'small' incidents — patterns emerge from small ones.
  • Blameful postmortem culture — kills learning and morale.

Quick recap

Define launch criteria. Stage rollouts with monitoring. Respond to incidents calmly: mitigate, then fix. Run blameless postmortems and act on them.

Glossary

Canary
Small initial deploy to detect issues before full rollout.
Postmortem
Blameless written analysis of an incident.
SLO
Service Level Objective; target metric like 99.9% uptime.

After shipping, requirements feedback should FEED THE BACKLOG for the next iteration — shipped is the start of learning, not the end of the conversation.

📊 FIGURE — what "ready to launch" actually includes
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two launch items that get asked about directly. Pre-defined KPIs let the team decide objectively whether the release succeeded, instead of re-litigating the goalposts afterwards. Hotfix readiness — having people and a path to ship a critical fix quickly — is part of launching, not a separate phase.
"}, "D687/ch6/s1": {"title": "Project Charter and Vision", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
CharterFoundational document defining the project.
SponsorSenior stakeholder accountable for the project.
ScopeWhat is in and out of the project.
Out-of-scope items are explicitly LISTEDwriting down what you will NOT build prevents misunderstandings and scope creep later.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — a one-page charter that aligns the team

WORKED EXAMPLE — the capstone charter, filled in
• Vision: “Club officers manage events and attendance in one place, replacing three spreadsheets.”
• Objectives (measurable): event CRUD + check-in by week 6; 20-user pilot by week 8.
• Scope: in — events, attendance, roles; out — payments, mobile app.
• Stakeholders & roles: sponsor (Prof. X, accepts demos); PO (Sam); SM (Lee); devs (all).
• Success criteria: pilot users complete check-in unaided; all PA rubric aspects met.
• Constraints/assumptions: 10 wks, free tier only, 4 contributors.
Every later dispute (“should we add payments?”) gets settled by pointing at the page — that’s what the charter is FOR.
⚠️ MEASURABLE OBJECTIVES OR EMPTY WORDS
“Build a great app” charters fail; “check-in works for 20 pilot users by week 8” charters steer. Same measurability rule as requirements — and the graded difference.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Projects without clear vision drift. A good charter is the contract between team, stakeholders, and reality — and it is what you go back to when scope creeps or priorities clash.

Core concepts

1. Project charter. 1-2 page doc: problem, vision, success metrics, scope, stakeholders, constraints, risks. Sign-off from sponsor. The reference for the project.

2. Vision and success. What does success look like? In measurable terms. 'Users can log in via SSO with 99.9% reliability and under 200ms latency at p95.' Specific, testable.

3. Stakeholder mapping. List everyone affected: users, sponsors, partners, ops, security, legal. Note their interest and influence. Engage proactively.

4. Sign-off. Get the charter approved before substantial work starts. This is the moment scope and budget are negotiated, not later.

5. Charter as living document. Update when scope changes, with explicit approval. Becomes the source of truth for what is in and out of scope.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Skipping the charter for 'speed' — pays back as misalignment later.
  • Vague success metrics — 'improve user experience' tells you nothing.
  • Forgetting to update the charter when reality changes — it becomes irrelevant.

Quick recap

A project charter aligns team and stakeholders. It defines vision, success, scope, and risks. Get sign-off; treat it as a living document.

Glossary

Charter
Foundational document defining the project.
Sponsor
Senior stakeholder accountable for the project.
Scope
What is in and out of the project.

Out-of-scope items are explicitly LISTED — writing down what you will NOT build prevents misunderstandings and scope creep later. The scope statement’s power is as much in its exclusions as its inclusions.

"}, "D687/ch6/s2": {"title": "Architecture and Technical Decisions", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
ADRArchitecture Decision Record.
Tech debtSuboptimal code/architecture taken on for speed.
Reversible decisionOne that is cheap to undo later.
Technical debtacceptable when it is intentional and tracked — a conscious shortcut logged for repayment, not silent rot.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — making and recording a technical decision

WORKED EXAMPLE — an Architecture Decision Record (ADR)
ADR-004: Database choice
Context:  relational data (users↔events↔attendance), team knows SQL,
          free-tier hosting required
Options:  Postgres (relational, free tier, team skill: high)
          MongoDB (flexible schema, team skill: low, joins painful here)
Decision: Postgres
Consequences: schema migrations needed; JSON columns cover the one
          flexible field; revisit if requirements go document-shaped
Status:   accepted (team vote 4-0, sprint 1)
Ten minutes of writing buys: no re-litigating in sprint 5, onboarding that explains ITSELF, and the PA’s “justify technical decisions” aspect pre-written. Architecture = the decisions expensive to reverse — document exactly those (stack, data model, auth, hosting), not every variable name.
⚠️ CONTEXT MAKES THE RECORD
An ADR without the constraints that drove it (“free tier, team knows SQL”) is just a preference log. Context → options → decision → consequences is the graded skeleton — same justify-by-constraints pattern as every other course.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Architecture decisions made in the first weeks shape the project for years. Document them, weigh trade-offs, and own them — bad architecture is expensive to fix later.

Core concepts

1. Architecture diagrams. Visual representations of system components and their interactions. C4 model (context, container, component, code) is a useful framework. Keep diagrams current.

2. Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). Short docs (1-2 pages) for each major decision: context, options considered, decision, consequences. Versioned alongside code.

3. Build vs buy. Build when it is core competency or no good vendor exists. Buy when it is commodity or specialty. Build is rarely cheaper than vendors think.

4. Tech debt management. Some debt is fine — it lets you ship. Track it explicitly. Repay before it compounds. 'We will fix it later' usually means 'never.'

5. Reversibility. Some decisions are easy to reverse (config); some are not (database choice). Spend more time on the irreversible ones.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Decisions made in chat with no record — six months later, no one remembers why.
  • Building everything from scratch — wastes time on solved problems.
  • Architecture astronauting — over-engineering for problems you do not have.

Quick recap

Document architecture decisions in ADRs. Choose build vs buy deliberately. Track tech debt. Spend the most thought on irreversible choices.

Glossary

ADR
Architecture Decision Record.
Tech debt
Suboptimal code/architecture taken on for speed.
Reversible decision
One that is cheap to undo later.

Technical debt is acceptable when it is intentional and tracked — a conscious shortcut logged for repayment, not silent rot. Service boundaries should follow business domains (orders, billing), not technical layers. API versioning prevents breaking existing clients when contracts evolve. Microservices tradeoff: you gain independent scaling and deploys but give up operational simplicity — a well-built monolith beats a badly-run microservice fleet.

📊 FIGURE — decision reversibility, and what architecture must cover
🎯 EXAM TIP
One-way-door decisions are the ones that are hard to reverse, so they deserve more deliberation; two-way doors should be made quickly. Separately, architecture must explicitly address the non-functional requirements — performance, security, scalability and observability — because these are the qualities you cannot bolt on afterwards.
"}, "D687/ch6/s3": {"title": "Implementation, Demo, and Handoff", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
RunbookOperations guide for handling production issues.
DemoLive walkthrough of working software.
HandoffTransfer of project knowledge and ownership.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most of project time is implementation, demos, and handoff. Doing each well — iterative work, clear demos, clean handoff — determines whether the project actually delivers value.

Core concepts

1. Iterative implementation. Build in small slices. Demo each slice. Course-correct based on feedback. Avoid big-bang launches that surprise stakeholders.

2. Effective demos. Show working software, not slides. Walk through user value, not implementation. Capture feedback live. Schedule follow-ups for design decisions.

3. Documentation for handoff. README, architecture overview, runbook for operations, contact info, known issues. Future maintainers (including future you) will thank you.

4. Knowledge transfer. Pair sessions, recorded walkthroughs, written guides. Cover: how to set up dev env, how to debug, what is intentional vs accidental.

5. Closing out a project. Final demo to stakeholders. Postmortem on the project itself: what went well, what did not, what to do differently. Celebrate; teams need it.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Working in isolation for months and then 'big revealing' to stakeholders — feedback comes too late to incorporate.
  • Documenting only the happy path — handoff fails when problems arise.
  • Skipping the project retro — same problems repeat next time.

Quick recap

Implement iteratively. Demo working software. Document for handoff: setup, runbook, known issues. Close out with a project-level retro and recognition.

Glossary

Runbook
Operations guide for handling production issues.
Demo
Live walkthrough of working software.
Handoff
Transfer of project knowledge and ownership.

Tailor the demo to the audience: executives want outcomes and metrics, developers want architecture, users want their workflow — one demo cannot serve all three unchanged. Each iteration should deliver visible value or learning — hidden progress is indistinguishable from no progress. Live demos need local fallbacks for the risky parts: networks die precisely when stakeholders are watching; rehearse with the fallback once.

📊 FIGURE — triage as a continuous activity
🎯 EXAM TIP
Bug triage is the ongoing decision about which bugs to fix and when — it runs continuously through implementation rather than happening once. Ranking by severity together with frequency is what keeps a growing bug list from quietly setting the team's priorities for it.

"}, "D687/aistote/s1": {"body": "

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

"}, "D687/cheat/c2": {"body": "

📋 Agile and Iterative Development

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Scrum Fundamentals

⚠ REVIEW ≠ RETRO Review inspects the PRODUCT (demo, stakeholder feedback). Retrospective inspects the PROCESS (what we change next sprint). The exam swaps them constantly.

Kanban and Flow-based Work

Core concepts — 1. Kanban board. Columns represent workflow stages (Backlog → In Progress → Review → Done). Cards move left to right. Visualizes flow and bottlenecks.

Quick recap — Kanban is pull-based, WIP-limited, continuous flow. Visualize work, limit work-in-progress, measure flow. Choose Kanban when work is steady-state or operational; Scrum…

Glossary — Cycle time measures the time work is ACTIVELY being done from start to finish — the flow metric teams can most directly improve. Bottlenecks reveal themselves on the…

User Stories and Backlog Refinement

⚠ ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA = THE TESTS IN PROSE A story without testable criteria can t be verified done. The as-a/I-want/so-that format plus criteria is the graded template — options missing the WHY ( so that ) are…

Sprint Reviews and Retrospectives

⚠ NO OWNED ACTIONS = NO RETRO The graded answer shape: retros produce a small number of SPECIFIC, OWNED, FOLLOWED-UP process changes. We discussed feelings is the distractor.

"}, "D687/cheat/c3": {"body": "

📋 Version Control for Teams

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Branching Strategies (GitFlow, Trunk-based)

⚠ LONG-LIVED BRANCHES = MERGE DEBT Why did the two-week feature branch explode on merge? → main moved on; divergence compounds. Small, frequent merges are the graded principle across every strategy question.

Pull Requests and Code Review

⚠ BIG PRs GET RUBBER-STAMPED A 2,000-line PR gets LGTM because nobody can actually review it — small PRs get REAL review. What improves review quality most? → smaller changes, every time.

Merge Conflicts and Resolution

⚠ NEVER PICK A SIDE BLIND Accept yours wholesale deletes a teammate s work silently. The graded behavior: read both changes, preserve both intents (or talk), test before committing.

Tagging, Releases, and Hotfixes

⚠ HOTFIX FROM THE TAG, NOT FROM MAIN Branching the fix from main would ship unfinished v1.3 work to production. Branch from the released tag; merge back to main after. Both directions are exam-tested.

"}, "D687/cheat/c4": {"body": "

📋 Code Quality and Continuous Integration

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Code Style and Linting

⚠ FORMATTER ≠ LINTER Formatter rewrites layout (spacing/wrapping); linter flags suspicious CODE (potential bugs, smells). Which catches the unused variable? → the linter. Exams test the split.

Unit, Integration, and E2E Testing

⚠ E2E FAILURES DON T LOCALIZE An E2E red says something broke somewhere ; a unit red names the function. That diagnostic difference is WHY the pyramid is bottom-heavy — the reasoning exams ask for.

CI Pipelines and Build Automation

Core concepts — 1. CI fundamentals. On every push or PR, run: install deps, lint, test, build. Fail fast on errors. Block merge if CI fails.

Quick recap — CI on every PR with branch protection is the floor for serious teams. Keep it fast, treat failures seriously, and never bypass it.

Glossary — Typical pipeline stages: build → test → package → deploy , defined as pipeline-as-code in the repo. A build artifact is the packaged output (JAR, container image)…

📘 Deep dive: CI pipelines & build artifacts — Typical pipeline stages: build → test → package → deploy , defined as pipeline-as-code in the repo. A build artifact is the packaged output (JAR, container image)…

Code Review at Scale

⚠ THE BOTTLENECK IS USUALLY PROCESS, NOT PEOPLE Reviews are slow — what first? → smaller PRs + agreed SLA + automated checks, not review faster. Systemic answers over personal ones, every time.

"}, "D687/cheat/c5": {"body": "

Core concepts — 1. Go/no-go criteria. Specific conditions to launch: tests green, key metrics in range, monitoring set up, rollback tested. Document them before the launch window.

The tell is 'just one small thing' with the date unchanged.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Removing agreed features is descoping, a deliberate trade-off, not creep.", "2": "Unmanaged growth in scope with a fixed date is what makes projects miss; it is not healthy.", "3": "Better testing is quality work inside the agreed scope, not scope expansion."}}, {"id": "q5", "topic": "User research", "text": "Stakeholder interviews surface:", "options": ["Just complaints", "Random opinions", "Real needs, pain points, and desired outcomes", "Code"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Interviews are for eliciting the underlying need, the pain behind it, and the outcome the person wants, not for collecting feature requests.
