It is versioned and reviewed, not frozen on day one and not replaced by hallway conversation.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "A spec locked at the start goes stale the moment the team learns something.", "2": "An unversioned document cannot be reviewed or trusted as authoritative.", "3": "Verbal agreements leave no record for the people who join later."}}, {"id": "q12", "topic": "Sign-off", "text": "Sign-off on requirements:", "options": ["Is permanent and immutable", "Marks alignment among stakeholders", "Replaces tests", "Is unnecessary"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Sign-off equals explicit alignment moment.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Sign-off records agreement at a point in time; requirements can still change through change control.", "2": "Agreement about intent says nothing about whether the built system works.", "3": "Without an explicit alignment moment, stakeholders discover disagreements during delivery."}}, {"id": "q13", "topic": "Personas", "text": "User personas help by:", "options": ["Replacing real users", "Auto-generating code", "Anchoring decisions to consistent user types", "Saving compute"], "correct": 2, "explain": "A persona is a composite user type that keeps decisions consistent: you ask what this user needs rather than what someone in the room prefers. Padding hides the important parts, and an arbitrary page limit drops real requirements.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Maximum length buries the decisions readers need in text nobody finishes.", "2": "A fixed one-page limit forces real requirements out of the document.", "3": "That sentence defines stakeholders; “responds in under 2s” = non-functional.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Age of a requirement has nothing to do with the functional versus non-functional split.", "2": "Comments document code; both requirement types exist before any code is written.", "3": "They are complementary but distinct: behavior versus quality constraints on that behavior."}}, {"id": "q17", "topic": "Ambiguity", "text": "“The app should be fast” is a poor requirement because:", "options": ["Too long", "Too technical", "It is not measurable or testable", "It mentions the app"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Replace with a measurable target like “page load under 2 seconds”.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "The sentence is short; brevity is not the defect here.", "1": "It contains no technical detail at all, which is part of the problem.", "3": "Naming the app is fine; the missing piece is a measurable threshold."}}, {"id": "q18", "topic": "Stakeholder input", "text": "Requirements should be gathered from:", "options": ["Developers only", "One manager", "Competitors", "All relevant stakeholders — users, business, support, compliance"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Missing a stakeholder usually means missing a requirement.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Developers know feasibility, not what the business, support, or compliance require.", "1": "One manager's view is a filtered subset of the real requirement set.", "2": "Competitor analysis informs strategy but does not capture your stakeholders' needs."}}, {"id": "q20", "topic": "Spec value", "text": "A written specification mainly serves to:", "options": ["Hide decisions", "Create a shared, reviewable agreement on what will be built", "Decorate the wiki", "Replace testing"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Specs surface disagreements on paper before they become code.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A spec exists to make decisions visible and reviewable, not to bury them.", "2": "A document nobody uses is waste; They deliberately avoid hours so the estimate stays about the work, not about who does it.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Points measure effort, not cost; converting them to money hides the estimate's uncertainty.", "1": "Points intentionally avoid hours so the size does not change with who picks up the work.", "3": "Bug counts measure quality outcomes, not the size of upcoming work."}}, {"id": "q2", "topic": "Velocity", "text": "Velocity is:", "options": ["Code lines per day", "Hours per task", "CPU usage", "Throughput in points per sprint"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Velocity equals points completed per sprint.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Lines of code measure output volume, and more lines is not more value delivered.", "1": "Hours per task is a time record; velocity is completed points per sprint.", "2": "CPU usage is a system metric with nothing to do with delivery throughput."}}, {"id": "q3", "topic": "T-shirt sizing", "text": "T-shirt sizing maps to:", "options": ["Coarse buckets (XS/S/M/L/XL)", "Exact hours", "Lines", "Bytes"], "correct": 0, "explain": "T-shirt scales convey rough effort fast.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Coarse buckets exist precisely to avoid pretending to hour-level precision.", "2": "Lines of code are an output measure, not an effort bucket.", "3": "Bytes measure artifact size, not the effort to build the item."}}, {"id": "q4", "topic": "Bias", "text": "Engineers tend to underestimate:", "options": ["Coffee", "Integration, testing, edge cases", "Their salary", "Big tasks"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The underestimated work is the part that is not writing the feature: integration with other systems, testing, and the edge cases. Estimate the whole path to done, not just the happy path.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A joke option; the systematic error is in non-coding work, not personal habits.", "2": "Compensation is unrelated to how teams misjudge task effort.", "3": "Large tasks look intimidating and get padded; it is the hidden small work that is missed."}}, {"id": "q5", "topic": "Planning poker", "text": "Planning Poker reveals:", "options": ["Salaries", "Lunch order", "Estimate disagreement that surfaces hidden complexity", "Code style"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Everyone reveals at once, so a wide spread shows that people are picturing different work. The value is the discussion the disagreement triggers, which surfaces hidden complexity before the sprint.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Estimation sessions discuss work size, not compensation.", "1": "A joke option; the reveal is about differing mental models of the work.", "3": "Style debates belong in review and linting, not in sizing a story."}}, {"id": "q6", "topic": "Reference stories", "text": "Reference stories help by:", "options": ["Rough ranges that improve as the work is broken down", "Increasing variance", "Replacing planning", "Anchoring estimates to known efforts"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A reference story is a shared, previously completed item that everyone agrees is a 3. Comparing new work to it anchors estimates to real effort instead of to each person's private scale.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "That describes how to treat estimates of vague items, not what a reference story does.", "1": "A shared anchor narrows the spread of estimates rather than widening it.", "2": "Reference stories make planning faster and more consistent; they do not remove it."}}, {"id": "q7", "topic": "Velocity range", "text": "Healthy velocity reporting includes:", "options": ["A range and trend over multiple sprints", "One number", "Random spike", "Ignored"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Single number is misleading; trend matters.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "A single sprint's number swings with holidays, illness, and scope, so it misleads.", "2": "An outlier sprint is noise; the trend is the signal you plan against.", "3": "Ignoring velocity leaves the team with no evidence-based capacity forecast."}}, {"id": "q8", "topic": "Time-boxing", "text": "Time-boxing risk research is:", "options": ["Avoiding it", "Allocating fixed time to investigate, then deciding", "Skipping research", "Endless analysis"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A time-box allocates fixed research time, for example one day for a spike, after which the team decides with what it has learned. It converts open-ended investigation into a bounded, planned cost.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Avoiding the risk is a different response; a time-box is how you investigate it cheaply.", "2": "Skipping research leaves the unknown in the sprint, where it costs far more.", "3": "Open-ended analysis is exactly what the time-box is designed to stop."}}, {"id": "q9", "topic": "Re-estimation", "text": "Re-estimating large items as you learn:", "options": ["Is dishonest", "Is forbidden", "Is normal and helpful", "Adds friction"], "correct": 2, "explain": "An estimate is a forecast, not a promise, so revising it as unknowns resolve is honest and makes planning better. Re-estimate especially after splitting a large item into smaller ones.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Updating a forecast with new information is honest; refusing to update it is not.", "1": "Nothing forbids re-estimating; agile planning expects it as unknowns resolve.", "3": "The friction is small compared with planning a sprint around a stale number."}}, {"id": "q10", "topic": "Cone of uncertainty", "text": "Estimates early in a project:", "options": ["Are useless", "Are exact", "Are best", "Have a wide cone of uncertainty"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Early estimates sit at the wide end of the cone of uncertainty because the least is known then. The cone narrows as work is broken down, so quote ranges early and refine later.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Early estimates are rough but still guide sequencing and feasibility decisions.", "1": "Exactness this early is false precision; the least is known at the start.", "2": "Estimates improve as the work is broken down, so the earliest are the weakest."}}, {"id": "q11", "topic": "Estimation pitfall", "text": "Forcing exact dates leads to:", "options": ["False precision and team distrust", "Faster CI", "Better delivery", "Cleaner code"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Precision implies certainty that may not exist.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Pipeline speed is a technical concern, unaffected by how dates are quoted.", "2": "A date presented with false certainty leads to missed commitments, not better delivery.", "3": "Pressure from an invented exact date typically pushes quality down, not up."}}, {"id": "q12", "topic": "Burn-down", "text": "A burn-down chart shows:", "options": ["Bugs", "Remaining work over time within a sprint", "Salaries", "CPU"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Burn-down tracks scope-remaining vs time.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Defect counts are tracked separately; it plots work done versus scope.", "3": "System resource usage is unrelated to scope tracking."}}, {"id": "q14", "topic": "Buffer", "text": "Including buffer in estimates is:", "options": ["Optional and unused", "Always wrong", "Lying", "Reasonable for unknowns and risk"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Buffer is the explicit allowance for unknowns and risk, and it is reasonable when it is visible and justified. Hidden padding is the problem, because it cannot be reviewed or reclaimed.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Buffer is deliberate and used when unknowns land; an unused allowance is not the idea.", "1": "Refusing any allowance guarantees the estimate breaks the first time something surprises you.", "2": "Stated, justified buffer is transparent; only hidden padding is dishonest."}}, {"id": "q15", "topic": "Communicating estimates", "text": "Best practice when sharing estimates with stakeholders:", "options": ["Share ranges with confidence and caveats", "Treat as deadlines", "Hide them", "Refuse to share"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Give stakeholders a range plus your confidence and the assumptions behind it. That lets them plan around the risk, which a single hidden number or a refusal to estimate does not.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "An estimate treated as a deadline converts a forecast into a commitment nobody made.", "2": "Hiding estimates leaves stakeholders unable to plan and destroys trust when dates slip.", "3": "Refusing to estimate abandons the planning conversation instead of qualifying it."}}, {"id": "q16", "topic": "Story points", "text": "Story points measure:", "options": ["Team mood", "Relative size/complexity of work compared to other items", "Hours exactly", "Lines of code"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Points compare effort relatively; velocity converts them to time.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Morale matters to the team but is not what a point measures.", "2": "Points avoid exact hours so the same work is not resized per person.", "3": "Lines of code measure output volume, not the difficulty of the work."}}, {"id": "q17", "topic": "Velocity", "text": "Team velocity is:", "options": ["Server speed", "Typing speed", "The average story points completed per sprint", "Meeting length"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Past velocity is the best predictor of future sprint capacity.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Server performance is a system metric, not a measure of team delivery.", "1": "Typing speed measures keystrokes, not completed, tested work.", "3": "Meeting duration is a schedule fact, unrelated to points delivered."}}, {"id": "q18", "topic": "Planning poker", "text": "Planning poker has everyone estimate simultaneously to:", "options": ["Pick a winner", "Save cards", "Skip discussion", "Avoid anchoring on the first opinion voiced"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Simultaneous reveal surfaces disagreement, which triggers useful discussion.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Estimation is not a contest; the goal is a shared, informed number.", "1": "The cards are a device for simultaneous reveal, not the thing being conserved.", "2": "Discussion is the point: disagreement is what the simultaneous reveal is meant to trigger."}}, {"id": "q19", "topic": "Estimate uncertainty", "text": "Estimates for large, vague items should be treated as:", "options": ["Rough ranges that improve as the work is broken down", "Exact promises", "Legal contracts", "Maximums"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The cone of uncertainty narrows as you learn; re-estimate after splitting.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Treating a rough estimate as a promise sets up a missed commitment.", "2": "Estimates are forecasts; contracts require commitments the team cannot yet make.", "3": "A range has both ends; using only the top or bottom discards the uncertainty."}}, {"id": "q20", "topic": "Padding vs honesty", "text": "When estimates feel risky, the professional move is:", "options": ["Promise the dream date", "Communicate the uncertainty and assumptions explicitly", "Silently pad 5x", "Refuse to estimate"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Visible risk can be managed; hidden padding destroys trust and planning.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Promising the date the stakeholder wants trades short-term comfort for a certain miss.", "2": "Silent multiplying hides risk, so nobody can manage it and the padding gets cut anyway.", "3": "Refusing leaves stakeholders to invent a date themselves, usually a worse one."}}], "D687/ch5/s3": [{"id": "q1", "topic": "Risk register", "text": "A risk register tracks:", "options": ["Salaries", "Bugs", "Identified risks, their likelihood, impact, and mitigation", "Source code"], "correct": 2, "explain": "A risk register is the living list of identified risks, each with likelihood, impact, a mitigation plan, and an owner. Score equals likelihood times impact, which is what ranks attention.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Compensation is an HR matter and never belongs in a project risk register.", "1": "Defects found are tracked in the issue tracker; risks are things that have not happened yet.", "3": "Code lives in version control; the register holds risks, owners, and mitigations."}}, {"id": "q2", "topic": "Risk score", "text": "Risk score equals:", "options": ["Likelihood plus Impact", "Effort times Time", "Cost only", "Likelihood times Impact"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Risk equals probability times consequence.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Adding the two treats a near-certain trivial risk the same as a rare catastrophic one.", "1": "Effort times time is a workload calculation, not a risk score.", "2": "Cost alone captures impact but ignores how likely the risk is to occur."}}, {"id": "q3", "topic": "Mitigation", "text": "Risk mitigation strategies include:", "options": ["Accept, avoid, transfer, mitigate", "Acting early to reduce a risk’s likelihood or impact", "Ignore, hide, hope, blame", "Only avoid"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The four standard risk responses are avoid, mitigate, transfer, and accept. Trap: naming only one of them, or listing coping behaviors like hoping and blaming, which manage feelings rather than risk.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "That defines mitigation alone, which is one of the four responses, not the whole set.", "2": "Those are coping behaviors; none of them reduces likelihood, impact, or exposure.", "3": "Avoidance is only appropriate sometimes; some risks must be mitigated, transferred, or accepted."}}, {"id": "q4", "topic": "Cross-team dep", "text": "Cross-team dependencies should be:", "options": ["Avoided always", "Surfaced and tracked, with explicit handoff dates", "Hidden", "Done in secret"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A cross-team dependency is a risk you do not control, so make it visible: name the interface, agree a handoff date, and track it. Hidden dependencies surface as blockers on the worst day.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Some dependencies are unavoidable; the job is to manage them, not to pretend they can all be removed.", "2": "A hidden dependency still exists and surfaces as a blocker when it is too late to plan around.", "3": "Secret coordination denies the other team the chance to commit to a date."}}, {"id": "q5", "topic": "Critical path", "text": "The critical path is:", "options": ["Daily path", "Test path", "Sequence of dependent tasks that determines project minimum duration", "Random tasks"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, so its length is the shortest possible project duration. Any slip on that chain slips the whole project; slack elsewhere does not.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A daily plan is a schedule habit, not the dependency chain that sets duration.", "1": "Testing is work on the schedule; it is only critical-path work if the chain runs through it.", "3": "The path is defined by dependencies between tasks, not by an arbitrary selection."}}, {"id": "q6", "topic": "Pre-mortem", "text": "A pre-mortem asks:", "options": ["Code", "What went well?", "Salaries", "This project failed — why? — to surface risks early"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Imagining failure surfaces hidden risks.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A pre-mortem is a planning conversation about failure modes, not a code exercise.", "1": "That is a retrospective question asked after the fact; a pre-mortem imagines failure in advance.", "2": "Compensation is unrelated to identifying project risks."}}, {"id": "q7", "topic": "Communicating risk", "text": "Communicating risk to leadership:", "options": ["Be specific, quantify if possible, present mitigation", "Hide it", "Use jargon", "Avoid the topic"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Leadership can only help with risks stated plainly: what could happen, how likely, how bad, and what you propose to do. Quantify where you can and bring the mitigation with the bad news.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Hiding a risk guarantees leadership hears about it later, when fewer options remain.", "2": "Jargon obscures the impact and delays the decision you need.", "3": "Avoiding the topic is how a manageable risk becomes an emergency."}}, {"id": "q8", "topic": "Tech debt as risk", "text": "Tech debt is a risk because:", "options": ["It is good", "It compounds and slows delivery plus raises outage risk", "It is unrelated", "It always pays off"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Debt equals future tax on velocity and reliability.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Some debt is a deliberate trade-off, but the debt itself is a liability, not a benefit.", "2": "Debt directly raises change cost and outage likelihood, so it is very much a project risk.", "3": "Debt only pays off if it is repaid; left alone it compounds."}}, {"id": "q9", "topic": "Single point of failure", "text": "An SPOF is:", "options": ["Optional", "A redundant system", "A component whose failure halts the system", "Healthy"], "correct": 2, "explain": "A single point of failure is a component with no redundancy, so its failure stops the system. Hidden padding is the dishonest version, because nobody can review it.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Buffer is meant to be consumed when unknowns land, not left as decoration.", "1": "Refusing any allowance guarantees the estimate breaks on the first surprise.", "2": "Stated, justified buffer is transparent; only hidden padding is dishonest."}}, {"id": "q11", "topic": "Risk reviews", "text": "Risk reviews should happen:", "options": ["Regularly throughout the project", "Only at end", "Once", "Never"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Risks change as the project moves, so the register is reviewed on a regular cadence such as each sprint boundary. A register written once and never reopened manages nothing.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Reviewing at the end only records which risks already hurt you.", "2": "A one-time review goes stale as the project and its risks evolve.", "3": "An unreviewed register is decoration, not a management tool."}}, {"id": "q2_d2", "topic": "Launch checklist", "text": "A launch checklist typically includes:", "options": ["Just tests", "Tests passing, monitoring, rollback plan, comms", "Just monitoring", "Random items"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Comprehensive checklists prevent oversights.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Green tests say nothing about monitoring, rollback, or communication readiness.", "2": "Monitoring alone tells you it broke without giving you a way back.", "3": "An arbitrary list defeats the repeatability a checklist exists for."}}, {"id": "q12", "topic": "Sign-off", "text": "Sign-off on requirements:", "options": ["Is permanent and immutable", "Marks alignment among stakeholders", "Replaces tests", "Is unnecessary"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Sign-off equals explicit alignment moment.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Sign-off records agreement at a point in time; change control still applies.", "2": "Agreement on intent says nothing about whether the system works.", "3": "Without an alignment moment, disagreements surface during delivery instead."}}, {"id": "q7", "topic": "Velocity range", "text": "Healthy velocity reporting includes:", "options": ["A range and trend over multiple sprints", "One number", "Random spike", "Ignored"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Single number is misleading; trend matters.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "One sprint's number swings with holidays, illness, and scope changes.", "2": "An outlier is noise; the trend is the signal you plan against.", "3": "Ignoring velocity leaves the team with no evidence-based capacity forecast."}}], "D687/cheat/c6": [{"id": "q1", "topic": "Charter", "text": "A project charter typically defines:", "options": ["Vision, goals, success criteria, stakeholders, scope, constraints", "Code", "Random scope", "Sprint plans only"], "correct": 0, "explain": "A charter is the short agreement that starts a project: vision, goals, measurable success criteria, stakeholders, scope with explicit exclusions, and constraints. It settles why and what before how.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Implementation belongs in the repository; the charter precedes the code.", "2": "Scope must be deliberate and written; unstated scope is where creep enters.", "3": "Sprint plans are execution detail below the charter's why and what."}}, {"id": "q16", "topic": "ADR", "text": "An Architecture Decision Record captures:", "options": ["Daily standups", "Code reviews", "Passwords", "A significant design decision, its context, and its consequences"], "correct": 3, "explain": "ADRs let future developers understand WHY, not just what.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Standups coordinate daily work; they are not a decision record.", "1": "Code review evaluates a change; an ADR records why a design was chosen.", "2": "Credentials belong in a secret store and must never be committed."}}, {"id": "q7", "topic": "Demo audience", "text": "Tailor a demo to:", "options": ["Yourself", "Whoever", "The audience — execs, devs, users have different needs", "No one"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Same product, different framing per audience.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "A demo aimed at yourself skips the audience's real questions.", "1": "Undifferentiated framing bores executives and under-informs engineers.", "3": "A demo exists for an audience; with none in mind, the framing has no anchor."}}, {"id": "q7_d2", "topic": "Constraints", "text": "Constraints include:", "options": ["Code only", "Just budget", "Time, budget, resources, regulations", "No constraints"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Constraints are the fixed boundaries the plan must respect: time, budget, available people, and regulatory rules. Naming them up front is what makes later trade-offs defensible.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Code is produced inside the constraints; it is not a constraint itself.", "1": "Budget is one constraint; time, people, and regulation bind the plan too.", "3": "Every project has constraints; denying them produces an unachievable plan."}}, {"id": "q3", "topic": "ADR", "text": "An ADR captures:", "options": ["Code", "Bugs", "A significant architecture decision, context, options, and consequence", "Sprints"], "correct": 2, "explain": "An ADR records one significant architecture decision with its context, the options considered, the choice, and the consequences. Drop the context and it becomes a preference log.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "The code shows what was built; the ADR records why that option was chosen.", "1": "Defects live in the issue tracker, not in a decision record.", "3": "Sprint plans schedule work; ADRs capture decisions and consequences."}}, {"id": "q1_d2", "topic": "Iterative implementation", "text": "Iterative delivery means:", "options": ["Small, regular increments delivered to users", "No delivery", "Big-bang at end", "Random delivery"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Frequent delivery beats heroic finishes.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Never delivering removes the feedback iteration exists to generate.", "2": "A single release at the end is the waterfall pattern iteration replaces.", "3": "Irregular delivery gives no rhythm for feedback or planning."}}, {"id": "q13", "topic": "Roles in charter", "text": "The charter typically lists:", "options": ["Project lead, sponsor, key roles", "Just CEO", "Engineers only", "Should be explicit and revisited"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The charter names people: project lead, sponsor, and key roles with responsibilities, so everyone knows who decides what and who to escalate to when blocked.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "An executive name alone does not say who leads day to day.", "2": "Engineers are part of the team, but the sponsor and lead must be named too.", "3": "That describes how assumptions are handled, not who the charter lists."}}, {"id": "q2", "topic": "C4 model", "text": "The C4 model views architecture at:", "options": ["Just network", "System Context, Container, Component, Code levels", "One level", "Just code"], "correct": 1, "explain": "C4 describes a system at four zoom levels: System Context, Container, Component, and Code. You choose the level that fits the audience instead of one diagram serving everyone.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Network topology is one view; C4 spans context, containers, components, and code.", "2": "A single level cannot serve both executives and implementers.", "3": "Code detail is the last C4 level, not the whole model."}}, {"id": "q17", "topic": "Handoff docs", "text": "Good handoff documentation includes:", "options": ["Setup steps, architecture overview, known issues, and how to deploy", "Inside jokes", "Only the code", "Old emails"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The next developer should be productive without archaeology.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "Inside jokes carry no operational information for the receiving team.", "2": "Code alone forces the next developer into archaeology for setup and deploy steps.", "3": "Email threads are unstructured and rarely hold current instructions."}}, {"id": "q15", "topic": "Definition of success", "text": "Beyond shipping, success metrics often include:", "options": ["Just code", "Tests", "User outcomes, business impact, team health", "Lines of code"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Shipping is an output. Success adds outcomes: whether users achieved the result, whether the business metric moved, and whether the team stayed healthy delivering it.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "Delivered code is an output; success is the outcome it produces.", "1": "Tests are a quality practice inside delivery, not a success measure.", "3": "Lines of code measure volume and reward the wrong behavior."}}]}
